title: Baquet, Sidney Bechet, John Reed and the Trixie Friganza story
summary: Russell describes Reed's ties to Bechet, Baquet's appearance and last years, his romance with Trixie Friganza, and brother Achille passing for white.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Yeah. For some reason, they called them bootleggers. It means that they were pirated. One of the labels is called Jolly Roger. And incidentally, Victor would press those things for those guys. They'd steal the Victor rights, you might say. They didn't steal anything directly because it wasn't the actual property. But they'd take the records off, copy them, and issue them on another record. And Victor was pressing their own material for other people, which they always refused to do if they knew it. But they never even bothered to check on it. But some of those things. Anyway, I was going to say that John Reed and his wife, Mary, Mary Caroli had been her name, were very close friends of Sidney Bechet. And he had arranged Sidney Bechet's recording for Victor. He had been there. We always called him in New York as his unofficial manager. Anytime they'd get a vacation, they'd go wherever Sidney was playing. There was one camp they used to call Camp Unity, which in those days had the reputation of being sort of a communist camp up in New York State. And Sidney would go up there, not that he was a communist. He cared anything about politics, as far as I know. But it was a left-wing camp. So he'd go up there and play in the summertime, maybe for a month or so, these camps. And John Reed recorded some of those bands on the job that Sidney played. And there's one thing which I promised, I hope I find it before I go. If not, I may get equipment up in Missouri that I can copy from. I'll have to later anyway, get a new amplifier. And I'll copy that if I don't get it done before, which Mrs. Rankin has asked about, a George Bakke and a Sidney Bechet duet that John Reed had recorded. On two clarinets, I believe. He might have played the sax. The time I heard George Bakke, he was playing tenor sax most of the time. Just a small, I have it in the notes, maybe four or five piece band. Nothing exciting at all. So anyway, Sidney Bechet had given the reeds one of his old clarinets. Once when he had so much trouble with his teeth, he thought he'd never play clarinet again. But then later, his brother fixed up his teeth, Dr. Leonard, and he did play. But anyway, they had one of his clarinets. One of them, I notice, has been given to the Jazz Museum here. But he undoubtedly had several clarinets. So we'll go over that Bakke. He looked like a sort of retired, successful businessman, you know. He was quite light in color and, oh, very dignified. And looked like he was, his health was well kept, you know. I mean, later on, I saw him when Bunk went to Philadelphia when he was on the way out, you might say, he'd gotten very thin and had been sick. And he came back here and died. Nobody ever really got to talk to him. That was about 1949, I guess. He came back here and died here within a year or so. And even had a sister here, and we tried to check on her last year. Got all sorts of rumors that she had a restaurant. For a while, they had a saloon up on the Rambart Street, South Rambart. But we gave up, finally, trying to contact any of the Bakke relatives. I'm afraid they were all gone. There was one cousin, rather a distant cousin, I'm afraid, George Henderson's wife, who gave us a little dope on George Bakke, too. Ramsey also had a very good interview on Bakke, which I double-checked the material on it. Not that I was trying to, but I mean all of his information. Checked pretty well with the things that he told Ramsey. Ramsey's interview was published in Downbeat. Quite a big article in Downbeat in the early 40s. After Jazzmen came out, we hadn't contacted him, I don't believe, before. Jazzmen was published. We didn't even know for sure where he was, although we'd heard rumors he was in Philadelphia. He had left the Creole band before the others, before Kepard and Big Guy, for instance, had taken his place after he left. There were all sorts of rumors about him leaving, that they had a big, more or less, disagreement someplace, and some of them were left standing on a railroad station, and others just walked off. I don't know what the story was. The story about George Bakke that is usually told too often not to be true. Evidently, this show that they traveled with, I can't think what it was. Was it the passing show? Anyway, that's all been written up, the show that he was with, one of the stage shows, Trixie Freganza, Town Topics, maybe that was it, something of that kind. Evidently, he had been her boyfriend. She seemed to fall for him. Who is that? For Bakke, Trixie Freganza.

Somewhere in my notes, I have an article when she died about, maybe in the late 40s she might have died, and I clipped that in the paper. I'll come across that. I don't think I put that in Tulane here anyplace, but we can get the dope on her life a little bit too. But the story, which is probably pretty accurate, because they'd always say, oh, they'd see me taking notes like Gigi Williams. Oh, no, you can't print that. You thought I was writing it up for an article or something. Don't put this down. But she locked him in a room once when the band was ready to leave town. She didn't want to lose him. So she locked him in her hotel room or something, and he couldn't get away. So I think that's when they sent for Big Eye. It was considered some sort of a scandal amongst the musicians, at least, and some of them didn't want to talk about it, not that it was anything unusual, I suppose, either, but it was in a way. So incidentally, George Barquet's brother, Scheele, passed for white for years. As early as 1937, when I was in California, a friend of mine, Campbell Holmes, I just have to remember the name, so he used to write for a tempo magazine, which was later sold out to Downbeat. It was a West Coast magazine, a music magazine like Downbeat. And he had tried to interview Scheele Barquet, but when he found out he was trying to write up something about his life for publication, he refused to talk to him. And anybody else that would go through town, and if he found out they were interested in New Orleans music, well, he'd clam up entirely. He wouldn't talk at all. He was a member of the white local out there. He'd played with Jimmy Durante when he went to New York. That band recorded for Jeanette, even. I think...
